content.text: Hopefully this gave you a peek into the operational research world of NSMRL!

SILVER SPRING, Md. - Rear Adm.  (Ret.) Tim Ziemer, the U.S. Global  Malaria Coordinator, President‟s  Malaria Initiative, visited the Naval  Medical Research Center ( NMRC ),  November 29, for a brief on the  current malaria vaccine research  efforts and to tour the facility. He was  interested in learning more about the  malaria program at the laboratory.  Capt. John Sanders, NMRC  commanding officer, provided a  general overview of the NMRC  enterprise with emphasis on the  infectious diseases research efforts,  specifically in the area of malaria.  “The NMRC malaria research  program is at the forefront of malaria

One notable collaboration is being spearheaded by  Cmdr. Jonathan Forsberg (NMRC, Operational and Un- dersea Medicine Directorate), who is working with a com- pany to explore a novel mode of anchoring prosthetics.  This project could produce important results for amputees.  Another collaboration being led by Lt. Roxanne Burrus  ( U.S. Naval Medical Research Unit No. 6 , Lima, Peru)  involves Duke University and focuses on evaluating the  effects of changing demography and land use on malaria  transmission. This is an important issue in light of the  prevalence of malaria in developing countries and is  important to the health of deployed war fighters. An addi- tional malaria-focused collaboration is being headed by Lt.  R. Vince Gerbasi (NMRC, Infectious Diseases Director- ate), who is using mass spectrometry to identify novel  antigens to be used as potential vaccine candidates.  Lastly, Dr Bjorn Song ( Naval Medical Research Unit-San  Antonio ) is leading a collaboration focused on exploring  the use of a synthetic oxygen-carrying fluid to reduce  tissue damage occurring in response to hemorrhagic  shock.

Since 2010, Navy biomedical researchers have been  collaborating with the Liberian Institute of Biomedical Re- search (LIBR) on two research projects funded by the  Armed Forces Health Surveillance Center/Global Emerging  Infections System (AFHSC-GEIS). These projects focus on  disease vector surveillance, detection of vector-borne viral  pathogens such as malaria, and vector control. The projects  are enabling the country to independently expand vector- borne disease surveillance and detection capabilities in Li- beria to benefit the Liberian Armed Forces as well as the  entire population of Liberia.

conversation.content: TikTok didn’t just change how we scroll—it rewired what we consider “watchable,” turning 15-second hooks into the new cultural currency. Now even Netflix trailers and YouTube explainers are getting shorter, not because creators want to, but because attention spans have been algorithmically conditioned. The real shift isn’t in platform design—it’s in our brains: we’re losing patience for slow burns, even when they matter. And while some call this adaptation, it’s more like a global recalibration of narrative value—where depth gets penalized unless it’s disguised as dopamine. Maybe the most dangerous part isn’t the format… it’s that we’ve stopped noticing how much we’ve lost.
conversation.subtopic: TikTok’s influence on short-form video trends and user engagement behaviors worldwide

conversation.content: I’m not convinced TikTok’s influence is empowering global storytelling—it feels more like it’s flattening it into a 15-second attention economy where depth gets punished unless it’s wrapped in viral bait. Sure, creators adapt by slicing epics into micro-reels or tagging rituals as “mystery challenges,” but that’s survival, not innovation. The real cost? content.text: Comparison with previous datasets S CI ERC is focused on annotating cross-sentence relations and has more relation coverage than SemEval 17 and SemEval 18, as shown in Table  1 . SemEval 17 is mostly designed for entity recognition and only covers two relation types. The task in SemEval 18 is to classify a relation between a pair of entities given entity boundaries, but only intra-sentence re- lations are annotated and each entity only appears in one relation, resulting in sparser relation cover- age than our dataset (3.2 vs. 9.4 relations per ab- stract). S CI ERC extends these datasets by adding more relation types and coreference clusters, which allows representing cross-sentence relations, and removing annotation constraints. Table  1  gives a comparison of statistics among the three datasets. In addition, S CI ERC aims at including broader coverage of general AI communities.

tion (37.9) signiﬁcantly beneﬁts when multi-tasked with coreference resolution (  $7.1\%$   relative improve- ment). Coreference resolution beneﬁts when multi- tasked with relation extraction, with   $4.9\%$   relative improvement.

We develop a uniﬁed framework (called S CI IE) to identify and classify scientiﬁc entities, relations, and coreference resolution across sentences. S CI IE is a multi-task learning setup that extends previous span-based models for coreference resolution ( Lee et al. ,  2017 ) and semantic role labeling ( He et al. , 2018 ). All three tasks of entity recognition, re- lation extraction, and coreference resolution are treated as multinomial classiﬁcation problems with shared span representations. S CI IE beneﬁts from expressive contextualized span representations as classiﬁer features. By sharing span representations, sentence-level tasks can beneﬁt from information propagated from coreference resolution across sen- tences, without increasing the complexity of infer- ence. Figure  2  shows a high-level overview of the S CI IE multi-task framework.

content.text: CAIRO - U.S. Naval Medical Research Unit No. 3   ( NAMRU-3 ) is playing an important role in medical research  capacity building in Liberia, which is recovering from a brutal  14-year civil war that devastated the country‟s infrastructure.

SAN DIEGO - The Expeditionary Medicine Modeling,  Simulation, and Analysis group at the Naval Health Re- search Center ( NHRC ) completed development of the Pa- tient Condition Occurrence Frequency (PCOF) tool. In Oc- tober, the tool was presented to the Force Health Protec- tion and Readiness, Strategic Analysis Working Group Of- fice of the Assistant Secretary of Defense, Health Affairs as  part of the verification, validation, and accreditation (VV&A)  plan for service acceptance. The working group forwarded  their recommendation for accreditation to the Force Health  Protection Integration Council. Once accredited, NHRC‟s  PCOF tool will be approved as the Joint patient occurrence  generating application.

Recently NSMRL acquired NAVSEA‟s new DP1/2 diving system. The DP1/2 is a surface supplied air system that  includes communications capability with the diver. This provides enhanced capabilities for underwater investigations,  since the diver can receive directions and report back in real time to the topside personnel orchestrating the experi- mentation. In return, NSMRL is testing the equipment for general Navy diving use and validating/revising operating in- structions for clarity, proper sequencing and procedural accuracy. NSMRL has a history of research in underwater  communications, and with the acquisition of this diving system, we harnessed another improved means of communica- tions with our divers.

The organization’s reliance on voluntary funding forces tough compromises—sometimes neutrality becomes complicity when partnering with regimes that exploit children. True evolution would mean shifting from crisis bandages to backing grassroots movements that dismantle root causes, not just manage symptoms. If UNICEF keeps designing programs in Geneva while sidelining community voices, it risks reinforcing colonial-era power dynamics under a humanitarian mask. The most uncomfortable truth? Saving lives matters—but without systemic change, it’s just delaying the next crisis. Until children themselves lead the solutions, UNICEF’s mission remains tragically incomplete.

conversation.content: Regional disparities in smartphone data consumption reveal more than just usage patterns—they expose deep divides in infrastructure, income, and digital literacy that shape how communities engage with technology. In urban centers, high-speed networks and affordable devices drive heavy streaming and cloud-based activity, while rural or low-income areas often rely on basic messaging and social media due to cost or coverage limits. These gaps aren’t just technical—they influence education, economic opportunity, and even civic participation, as those with limited access fall further behind in a digitized world. Digital strategies that ignore these disparities risk reinforcing inequality, treating all users as if they have equal bandwidth, devices, or digital skills. Companies and policymakers must tailor approaches—whether through subsidized data plans, offline-capable apps, or localized content—to meet users where they are, not where tech assumes they should be. Simply scaling global platforms without adaptation won’t bridge the gap; it’ll widen it. The real test of any digital strategy isn’t reach—it’s relevance across uneven terrains of access and need.

If market share growth in the EV sector is often hailed as a sign of success, why do some companies with rising shares still show flat or declining CAGR?  
Are we overemphasizing unit sales while ignoring profitability, innovation cycles, or supply chain resilience that actually drive long-term compounding?  
How much of the correlation between market share and CAGR is driven by subsidies, regulatory tailwinds, or short-term hype rather than sustainable demand?  
Could regional dominance—like Tesla in North America or BYD in China—mask underlying inefficiencies that drag down overall compound growth?  
What happens when a company sacrifices margins to chase market share—does that artificially inflate growth metrics without building real value?  
Why do some EV startups with modest market share outperform giants in CAGR, suggesting that scale isn’t always the engine of compounding?  
Is it possible that CAGR better reflects operational discipline and capital efficiency, while market share just measures visibility and volume?  
And if investors are chasing both metrics simultaneously, are they setting themselves up for disappointment when the two inevitably diverge?

Attention-based long short-term memory (LSTM) networks have proven to be use- ful in aspect-level sentiment classiﬁca- tion. However, due to the difﬁculties in annotating aspect-level data, existing public datasets for this task are all rela- tively small, which largely limits the ef- fectiveness of those neural models. In this paper, we explore two approaches that transfer knowledge from document- level data, which is much less expensive to obtain, to improve the performance of aspect-level sentiment classiﬁcation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our ap- proaches on 4 public datasets from Se- mEval 2014, 2015, and 2016, and we show that attention-based LSTM beneﬁts from document-level knowledge in multi- ple ways.

We run experiments on four benchmark aspect- level datasets, taken from SemEval 2014 ( Pontiki et al. ,  2014 ), SemEval 2015 ( Pontiki et al. ,  2015 ), and SemEval 2016 ( Pontiki et al. ,  2016 ). Fol- lowing previous work ( Tang et al. ,  2016b ;  Wang et al. ,  2016 ), we remove samples with  conﬂicting polarities in all datasets 1 . Statistics of the resulting datasets are presented in Table  1 .

In all experiments, 300-dimension GloVe vec- tors ( Pennington et al. ,  2014 ) are used to initialize  $\mathbf{E}$   and    $\mathbf{E}^{\prime}$    when pretraining is not conducted for weight initialization. These vectors are also used for initializing    $\mathbf{E}^{\prime}$    in the pretraining phase. Val- ues for hyperparameters are obtained from experi- ments on development sets. We randomly sample  $20\%$   of the original training data from the aspect- level dataset as the development set and only use the remaining   $80\%$   for training. For all experi- ments, the dimension of LSTM hidden vectors is set to 300,    $\lambda$   is set to 0.1, and we use dropout with probability 0.5 on sentence/document representa- tions before the output layer. We use RMSProp as the optimizer with the decay rate set to 0.9 and the base learning rate set to 0.001. The mini-batch size is set to 32.

conversation.content: Market share growth in EVs can be misleading if you’re not looking at the underlying economics—some players gain units through aggressive pricing or subsidies but burn cash, dragging down their CAGR. True compound growth often comes from operational discipline, like BYD’s vertical integration or Tesla’s software monetization, not just volume. Regional dominance doesn’t always translate to profitability; a company might lead in China but lag globally in margins or innovation velocity. Startups with smaller shares sometimes outpace giants in CAGR because they’re leaner, more agile, and focused on high-margin segments rather than scale at all costs. The correlation between market share and CAGR is often inflated by temporary tailwinds—like tax credits or supply chain bottlenecks—that mask structural weaknesses. Investors chasing both metrics risk overvaluing visibility while underestimating sustainability. If you want long-term compounding, look beyond the headline share numbers and ask: are they growing profitably, efficiently, and with moat-building tech?
